questions.learningObjective: Explain how expectation can shape a reported outcome
questions.stem: In a wetland bird survey, observers count flushes after playback. Which situation most clearly shows an expectation effect?

options.text: Observers who expect few birds record more of the birds they do see
Observers record the flock size from memory at the end of the shift
options.misconception: Mistakes a memory error for an expectation effect

options.text: Observers visit the marsh at different hours across the whole week
options.misconception: Mistakes a schedule difference for an expectation effect

options.text: Observers use the same playback volume and speaker distance everywhere
options.misconception: Mistakes standardised method for an expectation effect

questions.explanation: An expectation effect occurs when what the observer expects to find changes what they record. Only the first option lets the observer's belief about abundance determine the count itself.

options.text: Every habitat is guaranteed a share of the sample, so no habitat is missed entirely
The number of quadrats required is smaller than for a simple random sample
options.misconception: Assumes stratification always cuts the number of samples needed

options.text: The estimate carries no margin of error because the strata are exhaustive

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a margin of error for a survey estimate
questions.stem: A survey reports that 68 percent of the sampled ponds held breeding bittern, with a margin of error of 6 percentage points. Explain what that margin of error does and does not tell the team.

answer.exemplar: The margin of error describes the uncertainty around the estimate arising from sampling, so the true proportion lies within roughly six percentage points of 68 percent if the sampling assumptions hold. It does not describe uncertainty from non-response, from misidentified ponds or from a flawed recording sheet, and it is not a statement about whether the ponds were surveyed correctly.

questions.explanation: The margin of error quantifies sampling uncertainty under stated assumptions. It says nothing about bias from non-response or faulty recording, so a narrow interval can still sit on a biased number.
questions.hint: Ask what the interval covers and what it ignores.

options.text: Repeat the sample, check for bias in how plots were chosen, then report the chance variation
Check for bias in how plots were chosen, repeat the sample, then report the chance variation
options.misconception: Audits the design before seeing whether the estimate is stable

options.text: Report the chance variation, repeat the sample, then check for bias in how plots were chosen
options.misconception: Reports an interval before investigating the source of bias

options.text: Repeat the sample, report the chance variation, then check for bias in how plots were chosen
options.misconception: Presents an interval as if bias had already been ruled out

questions.explanation: Sampling error is handled by replication, while bias is handled by auditing how the sample was drawn. Checking stability first keeps a biased estimate from being given a narrow band.
questions.hint: Replicate for chance, audit for bias.

29.5 percent, since 118 replies came from 400 questionnaires sent
options.misconception: Stops counting at the first wave of replies before the reminder

options.misconception: Uses the reminder group alone as the denominator

questions.learningObjective: Describe how stratified sampling balances coverage
questions.stem: A survey must cover two habitats where one makes up 90 percent of the area but holds the species of interest. First the team sets strata, then it allocates samples. Which allocation is defensible?

options.text: Allocate disproportionate numbers so the rare habitat is adequately sampled, then weight back
Allocate samples strictly in proportion to area so the sample mirrors the landscape exactly
options.misconception: Confuses proportional allocation with protection of rare strata

options.text: Allocate equal numbers to every habitat and report the pooled total without weighting
options.misconception: Ignores the need to weight strata back to the population

options.text: Sample only the habitat that holds the species of interest and ignore the rest
options.misconception: Abandons the survey of part of the population to fit the target

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify who is and is not blind in a field survey
questions.stem: In a trial of a mammal repellent, the field crew applies either the repellent or an identical-looking control to track stations. Explain why the field crew should not be told which is which.

answer.exemplar: If the crew knew which stations held repellent, their behaviour at the trap could change and their reading of scats, tracks and hair could be swayed by what they expected to find, so the measured difference would partly reflect the crew's expectations rather than the repellent. A coded layout removes that channel, provided the code key stays with someone outside the field team.

questions.explanation: An unblinded crew can alter its behaviour at the station and its reading of the signs, so the difference would partly reflect expectations. Coded treatments remove that channel.
questions.hint: Ask what the crew's behaviour and readings could follow.

That one of the two crews made an error in recording the egg masses
options.misconception: Blames crew error when the sampling plan explains the gap

options.misconception: Reads a sampling difference as a real population trend

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how expectation can shape a reported outcome
questions.stem: In a trial of a mammal repellent, people who receive plain water still report fewer animal visits than before the trial began. Explain how expectation alone could produce that pattern.

answer.exemplar: Participants who believe a repellent is present may change their own behaviour, for instance by treading more carefully or setting the camera differently, so they genuinely see fewer visits, and they may also report fewer because they expect the treatment to work. questions.explanation: Expectation can change behaviour and the reporting of it, so a control group may improve for reasons unrelated to the active treatment. Attribution to the repellent needs the comparison group handled identically.

questions.stem: A survey of badger setts draws 15 randomly chosen woods and searches every sett in each wood. Explain why the confidence interval around the sett count is wider than for the same number of separate single sett searches.

answer.exemplar: Searching every sett in a wood gives observations that share that wood's habitat and disturbance, so they are strongly correlated and contribute far less independent information than fifteen separate searches would. questions.learningObjective: Describe how stratified sampling balances coverage
questions.stem: A survey splits a region into altitude bands and samples each band in proportion to its area. Explain why this design was chosen rather than a single random draw of sites.

answer.exemplar: Drawing a single random set of sites would leave the small high-altitude band represented only by chance, and because the species of interest is concentrated there, the estimate could be badly off in one direction. Fixing a quota for each band guarantees that every part of the region appears in the sample, which removes that particular source of coverage error while keeping the design simple to analyse.

questions.explanation: Stratification guarantees each part of the region appears in the sample, so a small important band cannot be missed by chance. A single random draw gives no such guarantee when the target species is patchy.
